title: Surveying Current Generation in Metal Nanolayers: The Impact of Rust
abstract: Global energy consumption is projected to grow by nearly 50% by 2050. To meet this demand, researchers are exploring new materials which induce electricity by moving ionic fluids over electrically conductive or semi-conductive layered surfaces, such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, and dielectric-semiconductor structures. Some report an energy conversion of up to 30%. The Geiger group has discovered a similar system by flowing saltwater over thin nanolayers of earth-abundant metals, like iron, which are prepared in a single step over large areas. This phenomenon could be implemented under flowing water at water treatment plants, as well as in estuaries, fjords and even living bodies, to passively generate power and monitor the environment. However, the mechanism of current generation in this system has not been fully defined. Further development of mechanistic understanding is necessary to predict and control this potentially useful energy converter. To explore hypothetical mechanisms, assorted metal nanolayers were fabricated from transition metals using electron-beam physical vapor deposition. Each nanolayer’s capacity for current generation was quantified and compared to properties of the metal and its naturally occurring oxide. This survey suggests electron transfer between multiple oxidation states in the metal oxide greatly enhances current generation. With this knowledge, future work will explore how electrostatic interactions at the interface between the aqueous phase and metal oxide surfaces generate charge carriers, and to a greater extent when multiple oxides are accessible.
